cards.body: A variable is a labeled box that holds a value so you can use it later. let score = 0; creates a box named score, puts 0 inside it, and now you can read or change it anywhere in your code.
cards.title: Variables are labeled boxes

cards.body: Use let when the value will change (a game score). Use const when it won't (a birth year, a tax rate). Make const your default and reach for let only when you need change — your future self will thank you.
cards.title: let vs const

cards.body: Good names tell a story: score, playerName, isLoggedIn. Bad names hide it: x, data2, thing. You spend more time reading code than writing it, so name like a storyteller.

choices: Creates a variable named age holding 20
cards.explain: let declares the variable, age names it, = 20 stores the value. (Checking equality would be age === 20, with three equals signs.)

choices: Store a value under a name for later use
Run a block of code on demand
questions.explain: Variables are storage. Running code is functions; page styling is CSS.
questions.q: Why do you create a variable?

choices: Its value can never be reassigned
questions.explain: const locks the binding: one assignment, forever. (The value itself can still be a changeable object, but that's level 4 material.)
questions.q: What is true about const total = 50;?

questions.explain: Names can use letters, digits, _ and $, but can't start with a digit or contain spaces.
questions.q: Which is a legal variable name?

questions.explain: Quotes make it a string. 42 is a number, true is a boolean.
questions.q: Which of these values is a string?

questions.explain: let allows reassignment, so lives can drop to 2. const would throw an error, and you can't assign to a number.
questions.q: A player loses a life. Which code works?

flashcards.back: A named container that stores a value so your code can use it later.
let allows reassignment, const does not. Default to const.
flashcards.front: What's the difference between let and const?

flashcards.back: Letters, digits, _ and $. It can't start with a digit and can't contain spaces.
flashcards.front: What characters can a variable name use?

flashcards.back: Reassigning means giving an existing variable a new value, like score = 10; after let score = 0;
flashcards.front: What does reassigning a variable mean?

cards.body: A function is a reusable recipe: a named block of code you can run whenever you want. Instead of copying the same steps everywhere, you write them once and call the function by name.
cards.title: Functions are reusable recipes

cards.body: function greet() { ... } declares the function — it just defines the recipe, nothing runs yet. greet(); calls it. The parentheses are the go button; without them, nothing happens.
cards.title: Declare it, then call it

cards.body: Parameters (a, b) are the inputs a function expects. return is the output it hands back — and it stops the function cold. No return statement? The caller gets undefined.

choices: Runs add with 2 and 3, giving back 5
cards.explain: The parentheses call the function, 2 and 3 are the arguments, and return sends 5 back to the caller.

choices: To reuse a block of code by name
questions.explain: Functions package behavior for reuse. Storage is variables; styling is CSS.
questions.q: Why write a function instead of repeating code?

questions.explain: Parentheses execute the function. Without them you're just mentioning its name.
questions.q: How do you run a function named bake?

questions.explain: In add(2, 3), the 2 and 3 are arguments. Parameters are the matching names (a, b) in the definition.

choices: Sends a value back and stops the function
Prints the value to the screen
questions.explain: return hands a value to the caller and exits immediately. Printing is console.log's job.
questions.q: What does return do inside a function?

questions.explain: A function without return finishes and quietly hands back undefined.
questions.q: function hi() { } — what does hi() give back?

flashcards.back: Write function name() { ... } to declare it, then name(); to run it.
flashcards.front: How do you declare and call a function?

flashcards.back: The named inputs in a function's definition, like (a, b) in function add(a, b).
It sends a value back to the caller and immediately stops the function.
The actual values passed at call time — 2 and 3 in add(2, 3).
flashcards.front: What's the difference between a parameter and an argument?

cards.body: An array is an ordered list inside one variable: let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];. One name, many values, kept in the order you put them in.
cards.title: Arrays are ordered lists

cards.body: Counting starts at zero. colors[0] is "red", colors[1] is "green", colors[2] is "blue". Nearly every off-by-one bug you'll ever meet lives right here — respect the zero.
cards.title: Counting starts at zero

cards.body:
let scores = [10, 20];
scores.push(30);   // [10, 20, 30]
scores.length;     // 3

push sticks a value on the end; length tells you how many items there are. Two tools, endless uses.
push() adds to the end, pop() removes from the end, and .length counts what's inside. If you only memorize three array tricks, make it these three.

cards.explain: Index 0 is red, so index 1 is green. The second item lives at position 1, not 2.

questions.explain: Square brackets build arrays. Parentheses group expressions; quotes make a string.
questions.q: Which line correctly creates an array?

questions.explain: fruits[0] is apple, so fruits[1] is banana. Zero-based, always.
push appends and returns the new length, but the array itself becomes [1, 2, 3, 4].
questions.q: let a = [1, 2, 3]; a.push(4); What is a now?

questions.explain: length counts items: three strings in the array, so length is 3. (The last index is 2 — length and last index differ by one.)

choices: undefined, because the index is out of range
The last item, as a guess
questions.explain: JavaScript doesn't crash on a bad index — it calmly hands you undefined. (Which is exactly why these bugs are sneaky.)

flashcards.back: Square brackets with items separated by commas: let list = [1, 2, 3];
flashcards.front: How do you create an array?

flashcards.back: 0. The first item is always at index 0.
flashcards.front: What index holds the first item of an array?

flashcards.back: It adds a value to the end of the array.
The number of items in the array. (Not the last index — that's length minus one.)
